 ELECTION 2026: Who’s running, where to vote, what to bring – your VOTING guide for Beaufort, Jasper counties
 October 31, 2026 
 By Delayna Earley and Shellie Murdaugh 
 The Island News 
 Voters in Beaufort and Jasper counties will help choose South Carolina’s next governor, a U.S. senator and members of Congress on Tuesday, Nov. 3, while deciding local races that will shape law enforcement, public schools, county finances and growth across the Lowcountry.
 Beaufort County voters will choose a new sheriff, fill eight County Council seats and decide seven school board contests. Jasper County’s ballot includes contested races for probate judge, auditor and a County Council seat, along with unopposed candidates for other offices. Municipal elections will also give voters in Beaufort, Hardeeville and Hilton Head Island choices about their communities’ leadership.
 Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Anyone in line at 7 p.m. will be allowed to vote, according to the South Carolina Election Commission.
 The races on each voter’s ballot depend on where that person lives. Before leaving home, voters should visit scVOTES.gov to confirm their precinct, polling address and sample ballot. A familiar polling location or an older voter registration card may not reflect the latest assignment.
 More election coverage
 Links to more The Island News’ coverage of the races affecting 
northern Beaufort County can be found at the end of this story.
 What to bring and what to expect 
 Voters will be asked to present one current and valid qualifying photo ID: a South Carolina driver’s license; a South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles ID card, including a South Carolina concealed weapons permit; a South Carolina voter registration card with a photo; a federal military ID, including Department of Defense photo IDs and Veterans Affairs benefits cards; or a U.S. passport or passport card. Standard South Carolina licenses and DMV ID cards qualify. A REAL ID is not required.
 Voters who forget their qualifying photo ID may cast a provisional ballot, but must show that ID to their county voter registration and elections office before the election is certified for the ballot to count.
 Voters who cannot obtain a qualifying photo ID because of a reasonable impediment should bring their current non-photo voter registration card, tell a poll manager, sign the required affidavit and cast a provisional ballot. That ballot counts unless the county board finds grounds to reject the affidavit.
 At check-in, voters confirm their address and receive a paper ballot to insert into the ballot-marking device. After making selections, voters should review the printed ballot before inserting it into the scanner.
 Selecting a straight-party option does not make selections in nonpartisan races or on referendum questions. Those contests must be voted individually.
 Voters who cannot enter the polling place or stand in line because of a disability or being age 65 or older may qualify to vote from their vehicle. Voters who need assistance should tell a poll manager. A voter eligible for assistance may choose an assistant other than the voter’s employer, the employer’s agent, or an officer or agent of the voter’s union.
 Voters who have moved without updating their registration should contact their county elections office about whether failsafe voting applies. The options depend on when and where the voter moved.
 Absentee ballots must reach the county voter registration and elections office by 7 p.m. on Election Day. A postmark alone does not meet the deadline. Voters must sign the return-envelope oath and have their signature witnessed by someone age 18 or older – a notary is not required. Photo ID is required for in-person returns, and anyone returning another voter’s ballot must follow the authorized-returnee requirements.
 Editor’s note
 The Island News began its election reporting before expanding its coverage area to include Jasper County and all of Beaufort County. As a result, our more extensive candidate reporting has focused on races appearing on ballots in northern Beaufort County. This guide includes races and polling locations throughout both counties, with candidate and precinct information drawn from SCVOTES as of Monday, Oct. 26, 2026.
 Federal and statewide races 
 The following statewide candidates are running for offices that will appear on ballots in both Beaufort and Jasper Counties. Party affiliations appear in parentheses.
 Governor and lieutenant governor: Michael Addison and Candace Brewer (United Citizens); Walid Hakim and Arnold E. Karr (Green); Jermaine Johnson and Sam Skardon (Democratic); Alan Wilson and Mike Reichenbach (Republican).
 Secretary of state: Jason Belton (Democratic); Mark Hammond (Republican).
 State treasurer: Vincent Coe (Democratic); Curtis Loftis (Republican).
 Attorney general: Richard Hricik (Democratic); David Stumbo (Republican).
 Comptroller general: Tiffany Boozer (Democratic); Mike Burkhold (Republican).
 State superintendent of education: Baba Amin Ojuok (United Citizens); Ellen Weaver (Republican); Sylvia Wright (Democratic).
 Commissioner of agriculture: DeShawn Blanding (Democratic); Chris Nelums (United Citizens); Cody Simpson (Republican); Michael Sullens (Libertarian).
 U.S. Senate: Annie Andrews (Democratic); Darline Graham (Republican); Mark Hackett (Constitution); Kasie Whitener (Libertarian).
 Congressional contests serving the two counties are:
 U.S. House, District 1: Jenny Costa Honeycutt (Republican); Nancy Lacore (Democratic); Bill Reeside (Libertarian).
 U.S. House, District 6: James E. “Jim” Clyburn (Democratic); John Peterson (Republican).
 Beaufort County is in Congressional District 1. Jasper County includes portions of Districts 1 and 6.
 South Carolina House of Representatives 
 The state House races serving Beaufort and Jasper counties are:
 District 118: Bill Herbkersman (Republican); Bernie Scolaro (Democratic).
 District 120: Weston Newton (Republican); Debbie Subera-Wiggin (Democratic).
 District 121: Shannon N. DeLoach (Democratic); Shelley Gay Yuhas (Republican).
 District 122: Bill Hager (Republican); Korey Williams (Democratic).
 District 123: Jeff Bradley (Republican); Ann C. Shippy (Democratic).
 District 124: Shauna Bishop (Democratic); Shannon Erickson (Republican).
 Districts 118, 121 and 124 include portions of Beaufort County. Districts 120, 122 and 123 include portions of both Beaufort and Jasper counties. Voters vote only in the district assigned to their residential address.
 Beaufort County races 
 The Island News has published candidate questionnaires covering Beaufort City Council, Beaufort County sheriff, auditor and treasurer, County Council Districts 2, 4 and 5, and school board Districts 2, 3, 4 and 5.
 The sheriff’s contest pits Republican Doug Seifert against Democrat Alphonso Small Jr. Other countywide races include contests for auditor and treasurer, while Heather Galvin is the only active candidate listed for probate judge.
 Sheriff: Doug Seifert (Republican); Alphonso Small Jr. (Democratic).
 Probate judge: Heather Galvin (Republican), unopposed.
 Auditor: David Cadd (Republican); Carletha Frazier (Democratic).
 County treasurer: Scott Songer (Democratic); Maria Walls (Republican).
 County Council 
 Eight Beaufort County Council seats are on the ballot. The active candidates are:
 District 2: David Bartholomew (Republican), unopposed.
 District 4: Michael “JD” Andersen (Republican), unopposed.
 District 5: Lynn Gerson (Democratic); Joshua Hower (Republican).
 District 6: Carolyn Fournier (Democratic); Anna Maria “Tab” Tabernik (Republican).
 District 8: Kraig Gordon (Republican); Trey Judy (Democratic).
 District 9: Mark Lawson (Republican); Jannine Mutterer (Democratic).
 District 10: John Casey (Republican); Travis Ludwig-Hodges (Democratic).
 District 11: Elizabeth Galloway (Republican), unopposed.
 Board of Education 
 Seven Beaufort County school board races are nonpartisan:
 District 2: Genie R. Brainerd; Christopher Dantzler.
 District 3: Cynthia Gregory-Smalls; William Smith; Willie Turral.
 District 4: Dee Matthews; Angela Stephens.
 District 5: Victor Ney; Gwyneth J. Saunders.
 District 7: David Carr; Adrian Lewis.
 District 8: Carlton Dallas; Kate Nolan.
 District 10: Melvin P. Campbell; Elizabeth Hey; Gene Meyers.
 Soil and water and public service districts 
 These races are nonpartisan. Public service district contests appear only on the ballots of voters eligible to participate in those districts.
 Soil and Water District Commission: Daniel Lesesne Jr., unopposed.
 Hilton Head Public Service District, District 1: Ibrahim Abdul Malik; Lola Campbell.
 Hilton Head Public Service District, District 5: Michael J. Marks; Tim Smith.
 Hilton Head Public Service District, District 7: Frank Turano, unopposed.
 Fripp Island Public Service Commission: Gregory S. Counts; Daniel S. Robinson.
 Jasper County races 
 Jasper County voters will decide contested races for probate judge and auditor, and choose between two candidates for County Council’s Robertville Township seat.
 Republican Gene Ceccarelli is unopposed for the Coosawhatchie Township seat, and Republican Michael T. Skinner, known as Mike Skinner, is unopposed for county treasurer. The Robertville contest will fill the seat held by Chris VanGeison, who did not file for reelection, according to reporting by The Island News .
 The candidates in Jasper County’s local races are:
 Probate judge: Dixie S. Ford (Republican); Albert Buster Kleckley Jr. (Democratic).
 Auditor: LaVonnia Von Aiken Fisher-Brown (Democratic); Megan Carroll Horton (Republican).
 County treasurer: Michael T. Skinner (Republican), unopposed.
 County Council, Robertville Township: Camika Beaton (Democratic); Sam Woodward (Republican).
 County Council, Coosawhatchie Township: Gene Ceccarelli (Republican), unopposed.
 Soil and Water District Commission: L. Grover Smith III; Stan Wells.
 The two soil and water candidates are seeking two seats. Those races are nonpartisan.
 Municipal elections 
 Beaufort City Council 
 Four candidates are seeking two at-large seats: Thad E. Lane, Jared Madison, Josh Scallate and Grady Woods. The election is nonpartisan. Scallate is seeking another term; Councilman Mike McFee did not file for reelection.
 Hardeeville City Council 
 Three candidates are seeking two seats: Steve Fier, Valarie Guzman and Landon Papay. Guzman is the incumbent among the three candidates, according to reporting by The Island News . The election is nonpartisan.
 Hilton Head Island 
 The town’s nonpartisan municipal election includes the mayor’s office and Town Council seats in Wards 2, 4 and 5.
 Mayor: Dave Ferguson, Alan Perry and Palmer E. Simmons.
 Town Council, Ward 2: Patsy Brison and Josh Peeples.
 Town Council, Ward 4: Tamara Becker and Rick Ross.
 Town Council, Ward 5: Chuck Dowd, David Ellis and Rob Guthrie.
 The mayor is elected townwide, while council members are elected by voters in their wards.
 Beaufort County transportation questions 
 Beaufort County voters will also answer two related transportation questions, each with a separate yes-or-no vote.
 Question 1 asks whether to approve a 1% special sales and use tax for transportation projects, lasting no longer than nine years or until $780 million is collected, whichever comes first. The proposal allocates an estimated $326 million for intersection and safety projects, $205 million for widening projects and $249 million for resurfacing and dirt-road paving.
 Question 2 asks whether to authorize up to $450 million in general obligation bonds, maturing over no more than nine years and payable from the sales tax described in Question 1, to fund projects in those categories.
